title: A Crossing He Never Made
standfirst: Underneath the fractured planes of David Bomberg's In the Hold sits a hand-ruled grid and a dispute over what it actually shows: dockers, or the immigrant ship that carried his own parents out of Poland. It took the Tate fifty-three years to want the painting at all.

sections.heading: A Hold Painted From a Story, Not a Deck
sections.body:
Under the interlocking planes of ochre, green and rust sits a grid: sixty-four squares, ruled by hand, that Bomberg used to break the scene apart before a brush touched the big canvas. He used the same device on his painting Ju-Jitsu, and it survives, uncovered by paint, in the [Study for In the Hold](https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artworks/bomberg-study-for-in-the-hold-t00914) that hangs alongside the finished picture at Tate — proof the fracturing was a method, not an accident of temperament.

What the method fractures has been read two ways. Older accounts describe dockers unloading a ship, one worker in a flat cap picked out among the wreckage of limbs and cargo. The National Gallery's 2019 reassessment, [Young Bomberg and the Old Masters](https://www.studiointernational.com/index.php/young-bomberg-and-the-old-masters-review-national-gallery-london), reads it differently: steerage passengers, children among them, hands reaching upward for a way out of the hold. That reading ties the picture to Bomberg's own house — his parents, Abraham and Rebecca, had crossed from Poland to escape antisemitism before he was born in Birmingham in 1890. Bomberg left no note settling which account is right, and both now circulate. Given who painted it, the second is hard to unsee once you know it, whether or not it is what he intended.

sections.heading: A Prize From Tonks, Then Expulsion by Him
sections.body:
Bomberg was the seventh of eleven children born to Abraham, a leatherworker who had left Poland for Birmingham, and Rebecca; the family moved to Whitechapel when he was five. He trained as a lithographer before studying under Walter Sickert at Westminster School of Art, and it was Roger Fry's 1910 exhibition of Manet and the Post-Impressionists that gave him Cézanne. John Singer Sargent and the Jewish Education Aid Society helped fund his place at the Slade in 1911, where Henry Tonks counted him among a second 'crisis of brilliance' alongside Stanley Spencer, Paul Nash, Mark Gertler and Isaac Rosenberg — the poet who became his closest friend, and whose portrait won Bomberg the Tonks Prize that same year.

Two more exhibitions undid whatever the Slade thought it had trained into him: the Italian Futurists in March 1912, then Fry's second Post-Impressionist show that October, which brought Picasso and Matisse to London. By the summer of 1913, Tonks, Frederick Brown and Philip Wilson Steer had expelled him. The prize and the expulsion came out of the same three years, the same teacher, and, in a sense, the same painting hand.

sections.heading: Filed Under Cubism, Answerable to No One
sections.body:
This feature's own catalogue files In the Hold under Cubism. Plenty of surveys file it under Vorticism instead, and Bomberg himself would probably have rejected both. When he gave his first one-man show at the Chenil Gallery in Chelsea in July 1914 — fifty-odd paintings, The Mud Bath hung outside where, by one account, it startled the horses pulling a passing bus — his catalogue foreword named no movement at all. It named a method: 'I APPEAL to a Sense of Form... My object is the construction of Pure Form.' Roger Fry and T. E. Hulme reviewed the show well, and Augustus John helped broker sales to the American collector John Quinn. In the Hold was not among the paintings that sold.

Wyndham Lewis wanted him inside Vorticism's tent regardless. Bomberg declined to write for BLAST, and when Lewis staged the movement's one group show, at the Doré Gallery in 1915, Bomberg appeared only in a section marked 'invited to show' — present, but pointedly not a member.

sections.heading: What the Somme Took Out of the Grid
sections.body:
Bomberg enlisted with the Royal Engineers in November 1915, married Alice Mayes the following March, and went to the Western Front days later. His brother was killed in the trenches. Isaac Rosenberg was killed in 1918; T. E. Hulme, one of his few early champions, died the same year. Whatever case Bomberg had made for pure geometric form, the war made a competing case, in person, that he could not paint past.

The Canadian War Memorials Fund tested this directly. It commissioned Sappers at Work, a record of tunnellers at St Eloi, and rejected Bomberg's first version outright, unhappy with how far its geometry had abstracted the men. The version the committee accepted is far more legible — Bomberg painted himself into it, shouldering a beam, a small protest at working to someone else's brief. He kept reaching for the language of In the Hold for a couple of years afterward and never fully found his way back to it.

sections.heading: Out of Fashion in Three Different Countries
sections.body:
The 1920s and 1930s took Bomberg a long way from Whitechapel. The Zionist Organization helped fund four years in Palestine, 1923 to 1927, where he set his old geometry against the landscape tradition of Turner and Constable. He painted Toledo in 1928 and Ronda across two later stretches, worked in Cyprus in 1948, and spent the second half of 1933 in Odessa, resigning from the Communist Party the moment he was back in London. During the Blitz he painted Evening in the City of London, St Paul's holding the skyline above the wreckage; his only official war commission of the second war was a set of paintings of a bomb store, made in 1942.

None of it sold well. By the time he began teaching at Borough Polytechnic in 1945, where his students included Frank Auerbach and Leon Kossoff, he was already, by most museums' reckoning, a difficult case rather than a name. In the Hold sat wherever it had sat since 1914 — Bomberg died in London in 1957, in real poverty, a decade before the Friends of the Tate Gallery [presented the painting to the nation](https://www.timeout.com/london/art/young-bomberg-and-the-old-masters-review) in 1967. Ten years is not long as these things go; the fifty-three since it was painted is the number that stings.

sections.heading: The Forgotten Word Turned Around
sections.body:
'Bomberg was not an unknown artist, but a forgotten artist,' the critic David Sylvester [said at the Arts Council's memorial exhibition](https://www.tate.org.uk/research/tate-papers/21/curving-round-david-sylvester-and-the-rediscovery-of-david-bomberg) in 1958, a year after Bomberg's death. Sylvester then spent much of the next decade making the case stick: he pushed the dealer Harry Fischer to show Bomberg at the Marlborough Gallery, took a percentage on the resulting sales, and pointed to Auerbach and Kossoff's own rising reputations as evidence their teacher had been worth more attention than he got. Patrick Swift printed a run of Bomberg's own writing, the Bomberg Papers, in the magazine X in 1960. A 1979 Whitechapel exhibition and Richard Cork's 1987 monograph built toward Cork's own retrospective at the Tate in 1988.

The Mud Bath, In the Hold's louder companion from that 1914 show, is now the painting most people mean when they picture Bomberg at all. In the Hold took the quieter, slower route into the canon — bought late, read differently by each generation that has looked at it, still argued over. That argument, more than any settled label, is the part of the painting that has aged best.
